description: A study the King asked for and paid for finds that the House of Orange backed colonialism for centuries and earned the equivalent of nearly 576 million euros from it. Prime Minister Rob Jetten has ruled out new reparations. We also cover rising inflation and the G7's emergency diesel release, a court ruling on family reunification, tighter mortgage rules for older buyers and a planned tax on vapes. Then it's the Golden Calf winners, the optician that dropped Meta's "peeping glasses", and 75 years of Dutch TV.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The Dutch royal family backed colonialism for centuries and earned the equivalent of more than half a billion euros from it. That's the verdict of a study the King asked for himself. He calls the findings heartbreaking.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the prime minister has already ruled out new reparations.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's Saturday, the third of October. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I'm Sam, and this is Dutch Daily Briefing.

segments.title: The House of Orange and colonialism

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: We start with the royal family and its colonial past.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: This is the study the King ordered himself?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: He ordered it and paid for it. On Friday, about sixty researchers led by historian Gert Oostindie handed it to King Willem-Alexander in Leiden. Their verdict is that every stadtholder, king and queen, at least up to Queen Wilhelmina, gave colonialism active and unscrupulous support. That included slavery and the violent crushing of uprisings.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Stadtholders were the Orange leaders of the Dutch Republic, before there were kings. And the money?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Nearly 576 million euros in today's money, almost all of it through the VOC, the Dutch East India Company, and the Dutch East Indies, which is now Indonesia. They made almost nothing from the transatlantic slave trade, but only because the West India Company lost them money.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So how much of it is left?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Very little, the researchers say. Stadtholder William the Fifth fled the country penniless in 1795, and later fortunes were lost on investments in Tsarist Russia and the Habsburg empire.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Did the royals actually run colonial policy?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Rarely, the study found. The exception was King William the First. He largely ran it himself, and in 1828 he looked for ways around the laws against the slave trade. The most imperialist monarch was Queen Wilhelmina. She backed the Aceh War and the military campaign against Indonesian independence. Criticism from the palace only began with Queen Juliana, in 1948.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How did the King respond?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: He called the findings heartbreaking and confronting. He said he can't change the past, but he can make a positive contribution to the present and the future. He called the report a call to action. He didn't mention money.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And Prime Minister Rob Jetten ruled out new reparations. He pointed to the 200 million euros the government set aside in 2023 for awareness, remembrance and education.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: NiNsee, the national institute on Dutch slavery and its legacy, called for talks on repair. A foundation for Indigenous people from Suriname and the Caribbean said they'd been overlooked again. And activist Mitchell Esajas of The Black Archives handed back his royal honour.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: He said words about reconciliation aren't enough while economic and racial inequality persists.

segments.title: Inflation and the G7 diesel release

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now to your wallet. Inflation is creeping up again, and fuel's to blame.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How much?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Dutch inflation hit 3.4 percent in September, up a touch from August, according to a first estimate from CBS, Statistics Netherlands. Fuel and heating cost almost 14 percent more than a year ago, and electricity is pricier now too.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Any good news?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Groceries. They've been cheaper than a year earlier for two months running.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: But the CBS chief economist, Peter Hein van Mulligen, warns that energy prices usually show up in shop prices about six months later. He just doesn't expect a spike like 2022, when inflation here hit double digits.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Across the eurozone it's 3.8 percent, the highest in three years. Before the war in Iran it was just under two.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the advisory pump price for diesel and petrol is above 2.70 a litre, though on average people pay a bit less than that.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now the G7 has agreed to release up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves over four months. A big chunk of the diesel goes out in the first twenty days.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That followed pressure from Donald Trump. He'd threatened to ban US diesel exports to bring prices down at home before the midterms, and Europe now gets much of its diesel from the US. Diesel futures in Europe fell about eight percent on the news.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The Netherlands isn't in the G7, but it's already drawing on its own reserves under a deal from March, and it released another batch on Thursday. It hasn't said whether it'll add more under the new deal.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And there's no new cut to fuel tax. The cabinet is just phasing out the existing discount more slowly next year.

segments.title: Court backs stricter family reunification rules

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Next, a court ruling on bringing family members to the Netherlands.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Family reunification. So people granted asylum bringing over spouses and kids?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. The district court in The Hague ruled that stricter rules also apply to applications filed before those rules took effect. Two Syrians with what's called subsidiary protection brought the case.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Which means what?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: They aren't recognised as refugees, but they can't safely go home. Since June twelfth, under the EU's new Asylum and Migration Pact, the Netherlands has had a two-status system. People with subsidiary protection now have to wait two years before applying, and they need housing for the whole family.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the law has no transition period. So if you'd already applied under the old rules…

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: You're judged under the new ones. That's why the IND, the immigration service, turned these two down. When the rules changed, more than 19,000 people were waiting for a decision on family reunification. It's not clear how many of them have subsidiary protection.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: What did the judges say?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: They said the effects can be serious, especially for people who applied earlier. But they found the new rules don't break higher law or general legal principles. It's the first ruling on the new rules.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The lawyer is appealing, so the Raad van State, the Council of State, will have the final word. There's no date for that yet.

segments.title: Banks cut mortgages for older buyers

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Mortgages now, and some bad news if you're in your fifties.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Go on.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Rabobank and ABN Amro are cutting how much older buyers can borrow. From March 2027, Rabobank and its subsidiary Obvion will start counting your expected pension income fifteen years before retirement, not ten. With the state pension age at 67, that's anyone from 52.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And pension income is usually lower than a salary, so the maximum loan drops.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Rabobank will also factor in life expectancy. From 85, you can borrow at most 70 percent of your home's value. ABN Amro and its label Florius start on December ninth. They're keeping the ten-year line, but at 85 they'll cap borrowing at half the home's value.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why now?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: New guidance from DNB, the Dutch central bank. If a loan runs longer than you're expected to live, DNB treats that part like interest-only debt, mostly repaid by selling the house.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Cheerful. Who's hit hardest?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Self-employed people with little pension saved. The mortgage data firm IEX says someone relying only on the state pension may qualify for about 100,000 euros.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Ouch. Does this touch existing mortgages?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: At Rabobank, only if you refinance or change your loan. ING hasn't moved yet, but the sector expects more lenders to follow.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Vapes are about to get pricier, though not until 2029.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The government plans an excise tax on vapes and refills, on top of the 21 percent VAT. The rate hasn't been set, but the aim is to make vaping about as expensive as tobacco.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Young people. In the latest schools survey, more than one in five pupils aged twelve to sixteen had tried a vape, and four percent vape every day. Eelco Eerenberg is the D66 state secretary for Finance, basically the junior minister for tax. He called the figures shocking, and said the health of our children can't wait for Brussels.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: But he admits you can just buy vapes online or across the border.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Which is why he'd still prefer an EU-wide tax. If one comes first, the Dutch plan will be dropped. But that needs all 27 EU countries to agree, and in June the finance ministers shelved it.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So the Dutch bill should reach the Tweede Kamer, the House of Representatives, early next year. Separately, vape sales are expected to be limited to specialist shops from 2027 or 2028.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: In Amsterdam, residents have won a fight over Utrechtsestraat.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The shopping and restaurant street that runs off Rembrandtplein?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's the one. Het Parool reports the city has dropped its plan to make it one-way. The city had called the street unsafe, with more than 4,200 vehicles a day.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the neighbours weren't convinced.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: They feared traffic would spill onto side streets. They disputed the city's figures and did their own counts. A neighbourhood survey found most people felt the street was safe. The business group MKB Metropool Amsterdam objected too.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Do-it-yourself traffic counting. Love it. So what happens now?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Smaller fixes: an extra zebra crossing, changes at the Frederiksplein junction, speed checks, speed bumps and checks on loading and unloading. The Centrum district committee gives its advice on Monday, and then the final decision is made.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Maya, have you ever seen an awards show where the trophy's a golden calf?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Every year, Sam. The Gouden Kalveren, the Golden Calves, are basically the Dutch Oscars and Emmys in one. They just closed the Netherlands Film Festival in Utrecht.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And one film cleaned up.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Truly Naked, the first feature by Muriel d'Ansembourg. It won six of its seven nominations, including best film, director and screenplay.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: What's it about?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It follows Alec, an introverted British teenager growing up in his dad's low-budget porn business. It's about how porn shapes teenage lives.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Not exactly family movie night.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: No, but it's in English, and you can stream it now on Pathé Thuis and Picl.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: On the TV side, Basta won three, including best drama series. It's the Videoland series about Marco van Basten, one of the greatest Dutch footballers ever. He scored that famous volley in the 1988 European Championship final, which is still the Dutch team's only major title.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Chris Peters won best lead actor for playing him. Joe Speedboot was the favourite with nine nominations, but it won just one, for its lead actor Daan Buringa.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Ouch. And Halina Reijn, who directed Nicole Kidman in Babygirl, got the career award. She called herself a farmer's girl in Hollywood.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Best career summary I've heard all year.

segments.title: Hans Anders drops Meta's camera glasses

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Now, glasses that can film you, and an optician that's had enough of them.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Hans Anders, the budget optician you'll see on most Dutch shopping streets, has pulled Meta's camera glasses from its shops and webshop, for now.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The Ray-Ban ones? They look normal, but they take photos and video hands-free?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Those. They start at 419 euros, and a little light flickers when they're recording.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: A little light. Very reassuring.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Critics here call them the gluurbril. Peeping glasses.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Brutal. And kind of perfect.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Hans Anders pointed to the public and political debate. On Tuesday, the abuse victims' support group Offlimits and the campaign group The Firewall gave Meta two weeks to stop selling the glasses, or face court.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the same day the Tweede Kamer passed a motion asking the cabinet to restrict wearing them, with exceptions for medical use. But the cabinet is reluctant. It wants to wait for an EU assessment that's due this autumn.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Hans Anders had only sold limited numbers, though. And Pearle, Specsavers and MediaMarkt are still selling them.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So if someone's glasses start blinking at you on the tram, now you know.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Speaking of screens, Dutch television just turned 75.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Happy birthday, telly.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The first broadcast went out 75 years ago this week. It was ninety minutes, live from a studio in Bussum, introduced by the announcer Jeanne Roos. The main event was a live performance of a play, De Toverspiegel, The Magic Mirror.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Who was even watching?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: There were about 500 sets in the whole country, at 785 guilders each. That was around a third of an average year's income.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: A third of your salary, for one play!

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So thousands watched through radio shop windows or in cafés. The royal family watched at Soestdijk Palace.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the government wasn't exactly a fan?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Prime Minister Willem Drees wanted money to go into housing, not luxuries. He feared TV would distract workers and corrupt young people. And Father Kors, who headed the broadcasters, warned on air about television's harmful influence.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Warning about TV, on TV. So what changed their minds?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Philips, the Eindhoven electronics company. It threatened to start television itself. The government gave in, but only as a two-year experiment.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Seems to be going well. And it explains something newcomers find baffling: why Dutch public TV is split among so many broadcasters. That's pillarisation, or verzuiling. Catholics, Protestants, socialists and liberals each had their own institutions, so you got the Catholic KRO, the socialist VARA, and so on.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Media historian Huub Wijfjes says TV peaked from the sixties to the eighties, when big shows drew seven to eight million viewers. And he says it's still the dominant medium.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And if you'd rather get off the sofa today, here's what's on in Amsterdam. Start at the Oosterkerk in the eastern city centre. There's an antique, curiosities and vintage market from nine to five. It's free, and it's today only.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: From half past twelve there's the Camera Japan Festival at LAB111 in Oud-West, the biggest Japanese film festival in the Benelux. Arthouse, anime and classics, plus music, dance and food. It's the second-to-last day and times may change, so check their website.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And tonight, the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra plays the Ziggo Dome in Zuidoost at eight, with Iván Fischer conducting. It ends with Beethoven's Ninth, and the whole arena is invited to sing along to Ode to Joy.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: There's even an optional sing-along rehearsal at seven. Thousands of strangers singing in German. I'm in.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's Dutch Daily Briefing for Saturday, the third of October. I'm Sam.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And I'm Maya. Have a great weekend.
